title: Adon Olam
description: Adon Olam ("Lord of the world"), the hymn that closes Sabbath and festival services, in Hebrew to an old synagogue tune that Eliezer Gerovitsch harmonised in 1897, for 2 to 4 singers. It praises the Lord who reigned before anything was made and will reign alone when all is gone, who is one, without beginning or end; its last lines say: into His hand I commit my spirit, when I sleep and when I wake, and I will not fear.

credits.tune: old synagogue tune ("A. W.", alte Weise), as Eliezer Gerovitsch printed it (1897)

licence.words: public domain: medieval Hebrew hymn, author unknown
licence.tune: public domain: traditional, marked "A. W." (alte Weise, an old tune) by Eliezer Gerovitsch, printed 1897; Gerovitsch died 1913 (some sources give 1914)
licence.arrangement: original, written for Stackapella on the four voices Eliezer Gerovitsch printed for the opening strain (public domain: printed 1897; he died 1913 or 1914), adapted for 2 to 4 beginners: bars 1 to 2 and 5 to 8 keep his chords and bass (bar 6 with C under its C7 where he has B-flat and C, and closing on D minor where he has F over A, which keeps the voices free of parallels); at every cadence on the low D the alto rises D, E, F under the tune's F, E, D and the tenor takes his C-sharp, so the last chord is complete and the duet ends on a third (his alto sings D, C-sharp, D); in bar 5 the alto sings C-sharp, D, E in sixths under the tune and the tenor the seventh G (his alto holds G); bars 3 and 4, whose printed tenor runs are hard to read in the photograph, are our own voicing over his A-minor half cadence (F, C/E, A minor, E, A minor/E, E7, A minor); and bar 7's bass falls to F2 and G2 instead of his F3 and G3, to avoid a leap of a seventh. Under a slurred syllable each harmony part sings one note
licence.source: tune and harmony from Eliezer Gerovitsch, Schirej Tefilah, part II (for Sabbath and the three festivals), 2nd edition (Rostov-on-Don: L. Adler, 1897), No. 16, "Adon olom. A. W.", pp. 89 to 90 (plate L. 32), Moderato, four voices (soprano, alto, tenor in the treble clef an octave down, bass), one flat, D minor, 4/4: only the opening eight-bar strain marked "A. W." (the old tune he harmonised), printed with verses 1 and 2 under it, is used; his composed continuation (the tenor recitative "Vhu echod" and the choir after it) is not. Written here in D minor as printed. The strain carries four lines of the poem, so it is sung four times: couplets 1 and 2 ("Adon olam", "Le'et na'asa"), 3 and 4 ("Ve'achrei kichlot", "Vehu haya"), 5 and 6 ("Vehu echad", "Beli reshit") and 9 and 10 ("Beyado afkid", "Ve'im ruchi"); verses 3 to 6, 9 and 10 fitted by us to the printed underlay ("Ve-a-cha-rei", "Ve-hu ha-ya" and "Ve-im ru-chi" sung in full, a note to each syllable, as the strain's first line is; "le-ham-shi-lo" splits the eighths of bar 3). The words respelled from the print's Ashkenazi transliteration ("Adon olom ascher molach", "l'es naaso", "v'sif-o-ro") in modern Israeli pronunciation; the four-letter name sung as "Adoshem" on the same notes. Breaths written in: the fermata D at the end of each strain held three beats with a rest before the next, and "kol" before the last line of each strain gives up three quarters of a beat. Read from the photographs of pp. 89 and 90 at zemereshet.co.il ("Adon olam, the tune Gerovitsch spread").
